hits.match:
Hello.java, run as:  java Greeting Ann
public class Greeting

concept_edges.logic: A compile-time error is found by javac before the program runs; a run-time error is found while it runs.
main is written inside the class's braces, so java Name looks inside the class Name to find main.
The black-box view treats the command-line argument as the input string and what the program prints as the output string.
A data structure organizes many values of a data type; the array holds a sequence of values of one type.
Every variable is named by an identifier that follows the naming rules.
Valid indexes run from 0 to a.length - 1; any other index throws an exception when it is used.
A variable of type t is given a value of type t, often written as a literal.
The command-line arguments arrive in main's parameter args, an array of Strings.
The source file Name.java holds the public class, and that class must be named Name.
Comments are part of the program text in Name.java but are ignored when it is compiled.
A run-time error appears only while java Name executes, after compiling has succeeded.
When one operand of + is a String, Java converts the other operand to a String before concatenating.
println("s") outputs exactly the characters between the quotes and then ends the line.
+ builds a new String whenever at least one of its operands is a String.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Making every variable a double is the right fix for integer division.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Use int for countable things and double for measured ones; where a fraction is needed, make one operand of the division a double (or cast) instead of changing every type.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A variable declared int can hold 2.5 or "hi"; the type is only a label.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A data type is a set of values and a set of operations defined on them, so an int variable holds only int values.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: args[0] can always be read.
misconceptions.correct_rule: If you run the program without typing the command-line argument it expects, reading args[0] fails with java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: 0.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: command-line args arrive already typed, no parsing needed
misconceptions.correct_rule: args[0] is always a String, so Integer.parseInt(args[0]) is needed to get its number.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: "10" - 1 or "6" * "2" works because the strings look like numbers.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Arithmetic operators other than + are not defined for Strings; a String of digits must first be converted to a number, e.g. with Integer.parseInt.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: arithmetic + binds tighter than string-concatenation +
misconceptions.correct_rule: Both uses of + have the same precedence and are evaluated left to right, so "s" + a + b joins a and then b as text; only "s" + (a + b) adds them first.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a(i) accesses element i of an array.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Array elements are accessed with square brackets, a[i].

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The number of brackets in an array type or initializer is the array's length.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Brackets give the number of dimensions; the length is set at creation.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An array element a[i] is not a variable, so it cannot be read into directly or used inside another index, as in a[a[i]].
misconceptions.correct_rule: Each element a[i] is a variable of the element type and can be used anywhere a variable of that type can, including as an index.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An array can hold elements of any type.
misconceptions.correct_rule: All elements of an array have the declared element type.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The first element of a is a[1].
misconceptions.correct_rule: Numbering begins with 0; the first element is a[0].

misconceptions.wrong_belief: new int[n] has slots 0 to n, inclusive.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The slots are 0 to n - 1.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Using an array means every cell must be scanned.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Arrays allow random access: a[i] reaches one element directly, and a loop visits only the elements the task needs.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Assigns a new value to a variable declared final.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A final variable cannot be reassigned after it is initialized; the compiler reports an error.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Ends a StdAudio program with no System.exit(0), so the terminal hangs and needs <ctrl-c>.
misconceptions.correct_rule: In the book's setup, a program that uses StdAudio should end main() with System.exit(0).

misconceptions.wrong_belief: class name and filename are independent
misconceptions.correct_rule: A public class Name must be saved in a file called Name.java.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A comment line is run like a statement.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The compiler ignores comments: everything from // to the end of the line and everything between /* and */.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: compiling also executes the program
misconceptions.correct_rule: javac only translates Name.java into Name.class; the program runs only with java Name, and run-time errors can still appear then.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Doing exactly what the compiler message suggests will fix the error.
misconceptions.correct_rule: An error message is evidence that something is wrong, but its suggested remedy may be wrong; find the actual cause.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Code that compiles is code that works.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Code that compiles can still have run-time and logical errors.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The computer fills in omitted steps or values that the programmer meant, e.g. REPEAT 4 [FORWARD 30] draws a square without a turn command.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The computer executes only what the code states; every needed step and value must be written.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: int[] a; already makes an array that can be indexed.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The declaration only names the array; until new (or an initializer) creates it, using a[i] gives a 'variable might not have been initialized' compile-time error.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: int x; without a value sets aside no memory; the variable only exists once something is assigned.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A declaration creates the variable (its storage) with its type; assignment later puts a value in it.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: System.out.println(5 / 0); is rejected by the compiler.
misconceptions.correct_rule: It compiles; the ArithmeticException happens when the program runs.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: After i changes, X[i] still refers to the element at the old value of i.
misconceptions.correct_rule: a[i] is evaluated with the current value of i each time it is used.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: X[i] names the whole array, not one element.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The array is a; a[i] is the single element at index i.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: == compares contents (the String == bug)
misconceptions.correct_rule: s == t is true only when s and t refer to the same object; s.equals(t) compares the text.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: .equals() compares references, not contents
misconceptions.correct_rule: s.equals(t) checks whether the two Strings contain the same characters.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The line number in a javac error is always the line that has the mistake.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The compiler reports where it noticed the problem, which can be after the real fault; for example, omitting the second left brace of HelloWorld produces errors reported on later lines.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The first command-line argument is args[1].
misconceptions.correct_rule: Counting starts at 0: the first argument is args[0], the second args[1].

misconceptions.wrong_belief: System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Java is case-sensitive: names of variables, methods and classes that differ only in capitalization are different names.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Indents nested blocks inconsistently, so the visual nesting differs from the real nesting.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Indent consistently, one level deeper for each nested block, so the layout shows the real nesting; the compiler ignores indentation.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: i and a[i] are the same thing, so the position is the stored value.
misconceptions.correct_rule: i is a position; a[i] is the value stored at that position.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: StdIn.readInt() accepts any typed text such as abc or 12.2.
misconceptions.correct_rule: If the next token is not an int (e.g. abc, 12.2, true), StdIn.readInt() throws a NumberFormatException at run time (Scanner.nextInt throws InputMismatchException).

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a large integer literal is automatically long
misconceptions.correct_rule: A sequence of digits is an int literal only if its value falls within the int range; for larger values the book advises the long type.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A variable declared inside a block can be used anywhere in the program, like a global.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A local variable exists only from its declaration to the end of its block.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: local variables get a default value on their own
misconceptions.correct_rule: A local variable has no value until it is assigned, and using it before then does not compile.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a variable declared in the loop body lives across all iterations
misconceptions.correct_rule: A variable declared inside the body is created anew on every pass and does not keep the previous pass's value.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Some statements inside the braces of a loop body are not repeated; they run once, before or after the loop.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Every statement inside the loop braces is part of the body and runs on every pass.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: public static void main() is an acceptable entry point.
misconceptions.correct_rule: main is written public static void main(String[] args); these keywords and the args parameter are required.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: sqrt(x) calls the square-root method.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Library methods are called with the class name, e.g. Math.sqrt(x).

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Omits braces around a single-statement body of if, for or while.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Braces are optional for a single-statement body, but using them anyway avoids bugs when statements are added later.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Leaves out a required keyword such as static or class.
misconceptions.correct_rule: public class Name and public static void main(String[] args) need their keywords, which are required; omitting or misspelling one is an error, usually caught by the compiler as a syntax error.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Writes Sytem.out.prinln or a misspelled variable name.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Every name must be spelled exactly, including capitalization.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A variable can contain more than one value.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A variable holds exactly one value at a time; assigning a new value replaces the old one.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Naming a variable max (or average) makes it hold the largest value (or the average) without code that computes it.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A name only labels the variable for human readers; only the statements that assign to it decide its value.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: new int[n] with a negative n creates an empty array.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Creating an array with a negative length throws NegativeArraySizeException at run time.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Java has no float literals
misconceptions.correct_rule: A decimal literal ending in f is a float; without the f it is a double.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Java has no long literals
misconceptions.correct_rule: An integer literal ending in L is a long.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: keywords may be reused as identifiers
misconceptions.correct_rule: Keywords are reserved by Java and cannot be used as variable names.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: null is an object
misconceptions.correct_rule: null means the variable refers to no object, so calling a method on it throws an exception.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: you need a variable to create an object
misconceptions.correct_rule: An object can be created and used directly without a variable, as in "s".length() or passing new int[n] as an argument.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: < vs <= and 0..n vs 0..n-1 are interchangeable
misconceptions.correct_rule: for (i = 0; i < n; i++) runs n times with i going up to n - 1; with <= it runs n + 1 times and reaches i = n.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: an out-of-bounds read returns null (it throws)
misconceptions.correct_rule: Reading any index outside 0 to a.length - 1 throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: () are optional on a no-argument call like println
misconceptions.correct_rule: A method call always needs parentheses, so an empty line is printed with System.out.println();.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Integer.parseInt works on any text, e.g. "five" or "12.2".
misconceptions.correct_rule: Integer.parseInt throws a NumberFormatException at run time when the string is not an integer written in digits.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: print and println behave the same (no newline difference)
misconceptions.correct_rule: println ends the line after printing and print does not, so print(s1); print(s2); puts s1 and s2 on the same line.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: println(s) prints a newline and then s.
misconceptions.correct_rule: println(s) prints s and then the newline.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Ends the output with print and expects it to appear right away.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Finish a line of print calls with println; some systems hold print output until a newline is printed.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: System.out.println("x is 5"); sets x to 5 (text inside the quotes is run as code).
misconceptions.correct_rule: Characters inside double quotes are printed literally; println only displays them and changes no variable. Only an assignment such as x = 5; sets x.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: printf() ends the line like println().
misconceptions.correct_rule: printf() does not add a newline; put \n in the format string to end the line.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An output statement that names the same variable twice (WRITE y, x, y) prints it only once.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Each expression in the output list is printed, so a repeated variable prints its value each time.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Reading a second input value into a variable that already holds one is an error, so the program cannot run.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A later read simply overwrites the variable's current value.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Writes a string literal in single quotes: 'Hello'.
misconceptions.correct_rule: String literals use double quotes; single quotes are for one char.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Writes / * comment * / with spaces inside the delimiters.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The delimiters /* and */ must be written without spaces.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A statement placed after the if statement belongs to its branch, so it runs only when the condition is true.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The branch ends at its closing brace (or after its single statement); the next statement runs whatever the condition was.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A statement written after the loop is repeated with the loop body.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The body ends at the closing brace (or after its single statement); code after it runs once, after the loop ends.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a statement runs without the ;
misconceptions.correct_rule: Each statement must end with ;, otherwise javac reports ';' expected.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: String is a primitive type like int.
misconceptions.correct_rule: String is not a primitive type; it is a class whose values are objects, although Java gives it some built-in support (literals, +).

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a string literal isn't a String object until the constructor is called
misconceptions.correct_rule: A string literal is already a String object, so "text".length() works directly.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Breaks a string literal across two lines of code.
misconceptions.correct_rule: String literals must not span more than one line of a program.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: name.toUpperCase(); changes name.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Strings are immutable: String methods return a new String, which must be assigned, e.g. name = name.toUpperCase();

misconceptions.wrong_belief: 2 + 3 + "bc" and "bc" + 2 + 3 give the same text.
misconceptions.correct_rule: + is evaluated left to right: 2 + 3 + "bc" is "5bc" but "bc" + 2 + 3 is "bc23".

misconceptions.wrong_belief: + with a String turns the whole other side into a string first
misconceptions.correct_rule: The expression (a + b) is evaluated first, and its value is then turned into text and joined to s.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: s < t compares two Strings alphabetically.
misconceptions.correct_rule: < and > are defined only for primitive types; comparing Strings with them does not compile.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A missing { or } is harmless.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Every { must be matched by a } so the class body and the method body are well formed.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Opens a comment with /* and never closes it.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A /* comment is the text between /* and */, so the closing */ is required.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A string literal can be left without its closing quote.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A String literal is enclosed in a pair of double quotes.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Uses a variable that was never declared, or under a different name (studentTotal vs total).
misconceptions.correct_rule: Every variable must be declared, and used with exactly the declared name.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A variable keeps its first value after a new assignment (the static model).
misconceptions.correct_rule: Each assignment or read replaces the variable's current value.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The computer recognises that one variable plays two roles, e.g. input value and running total, and keeps the values apart; it knows which variable is the counter and which the sum.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A variable holds one value at a time; each role (input, counter, running total) needs its own variable and explicit update.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: = stores the expression itself, not its computed value
misconceptions.correct_rule: y = x + k; stores the value that x + k has at that moment, so later changes to x do not change y.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a reference variable holds the whole object, not a reference
misconceptions.correct_rule: A reference variable holds only a reference to the object, which is stored separately.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: 207. and 2.3e4 are int values because they are whole numbers.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A decimal point or scientific notation makes the literal a double.

mis_edges.twin_logic: The array is a; a[i] is the single element at index i.

mis_edges.logic: i and a[i] are the same thing, so the position is the stored value.
mis_edges.twin_logic: i is a position; a[i] is the value stored at that position.

mis_edges.logic: A whole-number literal that is too big for an int automatically becomes a long.
mis_edges.twin_logic: A sequence of digits is an int literal only if its value falls within the int range; for larger values the book advises the long type.

mis_edges.logic: Java has no way to write a float literal.
mis_edges.twin_logic: A decimal literal ending in f is a float; without the f it is a double.

mis_edges.logic: Java has no way to write a long literal.
mis_edges.twin_logic: An integer literal ending in L is a long.

mis_edges.logic: 207. and 2.3e4 are int values because they are whole numbers.
mis_edges.twin_logic: A decimal point or scientific notation makes the literal a double.

mis_edges.logic: System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method.
mis_edges.twin_logic: Java is case-sensitive: names of variables, methods and classes that differ only in capitalization are different names.

mis_edges.logic: println with nothing to print can be written System.out.println; without the parentheses.
mis_edges.twin_logic: A method call always needs parentheses, so an empty line is printed with System.out.println();.

mis_edges.logic: print and println do the same thing, so print(s1); print(s2); puts s1 and s2 on separate lines.
mis_edges.twin_logic: println ends the line after printing and print does not, so print(s1); print(s2); puts s1 and s2 on the same line.

mis_edges.logic: println(s) prints a newline and then s.
mis_edges.twin_logic: println(s) prints s and then the newline.

mis_edges.logic: System.out.println("x is 5"); sets x to 5 (text inside the quotes is run as code).
mis_edges.twin_logic: Characters inside double quotes are printed literally; println only displays them and changes no variable. Only an assignment such as x = 5; sets x.

mis_edges.logic: class name and filename are independent
mis_edges.twin_logic: A public class Name must be saved in a file called Name.java.

mis_edges.logic: The computer fills in omitted steps or values that the programmer meant, e.g. REPEAT 4 [FORWARD 30] draws a square without a turn command.
mis_edges.twin_logic: The computer executes only what the code states; every needed step and value must be written.

mis_edges.logic: If javac Name.java finishes without errors, the program already works and has run.
mis_edges.twin_logic: javac only translates Name.java into Name.class; the program runs only with java Name, and run-time errors can still appear then.

mis_edges.logic: Code that compiles is code that works.
mis_edges.twin_logic: Code that compiles can still have run-time and logical errors.

mis_edges.logic: System.out.println(5 / 0); is rejected by the compiler.
mis_edges.twin_logic: It compiles; the ArithmeticException happens when the program runs.

mis_edges.logic: Integer.parseInt works on any text, e.g. "five" or "12.2".
mis_edges.twin_logic: Integer.parseInt throws a NumberFormatException at run time when the string is not an integer written in digits.

mis_edges.logic: print and println behave the same (no newline difference)
mis_edges.twin_logic: println ends the line after printing and print does not, so print(s1); print(s2); puts s1 and s2 on the same line.

mis_edges.logic: printf() ends the line like println().
mis_edges.twin_logic: printf() does not add a newline; put \n in the format string to end the line.

mis_edges.logic: An output statement that names the same variable twice (WRITE y, x, y) prints it only once.
mis_edges.twin_logic: Each expression in the output list is printed, so a repeated variable prints its value each time.

mis_edges.logic: In "s" + a + b, the numbers a and b are added first and their sum is joined to s.
mis_edges.twin_logic: Both uses of + have the same precedence and are evaluated left to right, so "s" + a + b joins a and then b as text; only "s" + (a + b) adds them first.

mis_edges.logic: 2 + 3 + "bc" and "bc" + 2 + 3 give the same text.
mis_edges.twin_logic: + is evaluated left to right: 2 + 3 + "bc" is "5bc" but "bc" + 2 + 3 is "bc23".

mis_edges.logic: In "s" + (a + b), the text a + b is joined to s instead of its value.
mis_edges.twin_logic: The expression (a + b) is evaluated first, and its value is then turned into text and joined to s.

mis_edges.logic: 2 + 3 + "bc" and "bc" + 2 + 3 give the same text.
mis_edges.twin_logic: + is evaluated left to right: 2 + 3 + "bc" is "5bc" but "bc" + 2 + 3 is "bc23".

mis_edges.logic: System.out.println("x is 5"); sets x to 5 (text inside the quotes is run as code).
mis_edges.twin_logic: Characters inside double quotes are printed literally; println only displays them and changes no variable. Only an assignment such as x = 5; sets x.

mis_edges.logic: "10" - 1 or "6" * "2" works because the strings look like numbers.
mis_edges.twin_logic: Arithmetic operators other than + are not defined for Strings; a String of digits must first be converted to a number, e.g. with Integer.parseInt.

mis_edges.logic: s == t is true whenever the two Strings contain the same text.
mis_edges.twin_logic: s == t is true only when s and t refer to the same object; s.equals(t) compares the text.

mis_edges.logic: s.equals(t) checks whether s and t are the same object.
mis_edges.twin_logic: s.equals(t) checks whether the two Strings contain the same characters.

mis_edges.logic: null is an object, so a method can be called on a variable that is null.
mis_edges.twin_logic: null means the variable refers to no object, so calling a method on it throws an exception.

mis_edges.logic: An object can only be created by first storing it in a variable.
mis_edges.twin_logic: An object can be created and used directly without a variable, as in "s".length() or passing new int[n] as an argument.

mis_edges.logic: String is a primitive type like int.
mis_edges.twin_logic: String is not a primitive type; it is a class whose values are objects, although Java gives it some built-in support (literals, +).

mis_edges.logic: "text" is not a String object until new String(...) is called.
mis_edges.twin_logic: A string literal is already a String object, so "text".length() works directly.

mis_edges.logic: name.toUpperCase(); changes name.
mis_edges.twin_logic: Strings are immutable: String methods return a new String, which must be assigned, e.g. name = name.toUpperCase();

mis_edges.logic: s < t compares two Strings alphabetically.
mis_edges.twin_logic: < and > are defined only for primitive types; comparing Strings with them does not compile.

mis_edges.logic: A variable declared int can hold 2.5 or "hi"; the type is only a label.
mis_edges.twin_logic: A data type is a set of values and a set of operations defined on them, so an int variable holds only int values.

mis_edges.logic: An array element a[i] is not a variable, so it cannot be read into directly or used inside another index, as in a[a[i]].
mis_edges.twin_logic: Each element a[i] is a variable of the element type and can be used anywhere a variable of that type can, including as an index.

mis_edges.logic: int x; without a value sets aside no memory; the variable only exists once something is assigned.
mis_edges.twin_logic: A declaration creates the variable (its storage) with its type; assignment later puts a value in it.

mis_edges.logic: A variable declared inside a block can be used anywhere in the program, like a global.
mis_edges.twin_logic: A local variable exists only from its declaration to the end of its block.

mis_edges.logic: int x; inside main starts at 0, so x can be used before anything is assigned to it.
mis_edges.twin_logic: A local variable has no value until it is assigned, and using it before then does not compile.

mis_edges.logic: a variable declared in the loop body lives across all iterations
mis_edges.twin_logic: A variable declared inside the body is created anew on every pass and does not keep the previous pass's value.

mis_edges.logic: A variable can contain more than one value.
mis_edges.twin_logic: A variable holds exactly one value at a time; assigning a new value replaces the old one.

mis_edges.logic: Naming a variable max (or average) makes it hold the largest value (or the average) without code that computes it.
mis_edges.twin_logic: A name only labels the variable for human readers; only the statements that assign to it decide its value.

mis_edges.logic: A keyword such as int or class can be used as a variable name.
mis_edges.twin_logic: Keywords are reserved by Java and cannot be used as variable names.

mis_edges.logic: Reading a second input value into a variable that already holds one is an error, so the program cannot run.
mis_edges.twin_logic: A later read simply overwrites the variable's current value.

mis_edges.logic: A variable keeps its first value after a new assignment (the static model).
mis_edges.twin_logic: Each assignment or read replaces the variable's current value.

mis_edges.logic: The computer recognises that one variable plays two roles, e.g. input value and running total, and keeps the values apart; it knows which variable is the counter and which the sum.
mis_edges.twin_logic: A variable holds one value at a time; each role (input, counter, running total) needs its own variable and explicit update.

mis_edges.logic: = stores the expression itself, not its computed value
mis_edges.twin_logic: y = x + k; stores the value that x + k has at that moment, so later changes to x do not change y.

mis_edges.logic: A String or array variable contains the whole object inside it.
mis_edges.twin_logic: A reference variable holds only a reference to the object, which is stored separately.

level_edges.logic: array bounds -> L0 (Prestructural): the answer holds a rule that contradicts Java (4 ways).

ways.edge_logic: Folk meaning: in English, 'items 1 to 10' or 'up to n' includes the end point, and reading past the end of a list just gives 'nothing'. Java rule: the legal indices are 0..length-1, and any other index throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of returning a value.
ways.exact_rule: Folk meaning: in English, 'items 1 to 10' or 'up to n' includes the end point, and reading past the end of a list just gives 'nothing'. Java rule: the legal indices are 0..length-1, and any other index throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of returning a value.
ways.boundary: Any correct, programming-specific statement about array bounds makes the answer L1 or higher.

level_mis_links.exact_rule: wrong rule: Making every variable a double is the right fix for integer division. Right rule: Use int for countable things and double for measured ones; where a fraction is needed, make one operand of the division a double (or cast) instead of changing every type.

wrong rule: A variable declared int can hold 2.5 or "hi"; the type is only a label. Right rule: A data type is a set of values and a set of operations defined on them, so an int variable holds only int values.

Points to LT (find each operand's type, then apply that type's operator). Applied unevenly, a student uses the int operator for 7 / 2 in one line (3) but real division in the next (3.5), or treats a String "12" as a number in one + and as text in another. (here mixing in: "Making every variable a double is the right fix for integer division")

Widening a variable's type (int to double) usually still compiles but changes which operations run: / keeps fractions and output prints 3.0. Narrowing it (double to int) breaks every assignment of a double value with a compile-time error. Values that fit both types are kept.
wrong rule: print and println behave the same (no newline difference). Right rule: println(s) prints s and then ends the line, but print(s) does not, so print("a"); print("b"); gives ab on one line.

Points to LT (output appears in the order the output calls execute, with a line break only after println). An uneven trace drops a repeated value, puts output lines out of order, or adds line breaks after print on some calls. (here mixing in: "print and println behave the same (no newline difference)")
wrong rule: printf() ends the line like println(). Right rule: printf() adds no newline. Put \n (or %n) in the format string to end the line.

wrong rule: An output statement that names the same variable twice (WRITE y, x, y) prints it only once. Right rule: Every expression in the output is printed, so System.out.println(y + " " + x + " " + y) with x=6, y=9 prints 9 6 9.
Switching System.out.print/println to StdOut.print/println keeps the output. Changing println to print keeps every character but removes the line break, so lines join.
wrong rule: Compiling also executes the program. Right rule: The program runs only when java Name is typed; javac only translates it.

Applies the run rule (LT: main's statements execute in order, one by one, each once) unevenly: e.g. executes the print statements in written order on one trace but skips one or reorders them on another. (here mixing in: "compiling also executes the program")

Running again with the same arguments reproduces the same output (for programs without randomness or input); changing the arguments changes the output without recompiling; editing the source changes nothing until recompiled.
wrong rule: print and println behave the same. Right rule: println ends the line after printing and print does not, so print(s1); print(s2); puts s1 and s2 on the same line.
wrong rule: println(s) prints a newline and then s. Right rule: println(s) prints s and then the line terminator.

Applies the println rule (print, then end line) unevenly: puts the newline before the text on one call and after it on another, or forgets that the next output starts on a new line. (here mixing in: "print and println behave the same (no newline difference)")
wrong rule: System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method. Right rule: Java is case-sensitive: names that differ only in capitalization are different names.
wrong rule: () are optional on a no-argument call like println. Right rule: A method call always needs parentheses, so an empty line is printed with System.out.println();.
Replacing println with print joins the next output onto the same line (a typical logic error); the characters printed stay the same.
wrong rule: 2 + 3 + "bc" and "bc" + 2 + 3 give the same text. Right rule: + is evaluated left to right: 2 + 3 + "bc" is "5bc" but "bc" + 2 + 3 is "bc23".

Points to LT (+ is applied left to right, each + deciding between addition and concatenation from its two operands at that moment). Applied unevenly: once a String has appeared the student goes back to numeric addition for later terms, or concatenates two numbers that come before any String. (here mixing in: "2 + 3 + "bc" and "bc" + 2 + 3 give the same text")
Adding parentheses around the numeric part changes "bc23" into "bc5"; moving a String operand earlier turns every later + into concatenation; the order of operands matters, unlike numeric addition.
wrong rule: The class name and the file name are independent. Right rule: public class Name must be saved in a file named Name.java.

Applies the containment rule unevenly: treats the class's closing brace as the end of main on one trace, or looks for main outside the class on another; the class body is everything between the outermost { and }. (here mixing in: "class name and filename are independent")
Renaming the class requires renaming the file (and the java command) to keep it compiling and runnable; moving main outside the class braces breaks compilation.

wrong rule: int[] a; already makes an array that can be indexed. Right rule: The declaration only names the array variable; until new (or an initializer) creates the array, a[i] gives the compile-time error 'variable a might not have been initialized'.
wrong rule: An array can hold elements of any type. Right rule: Every element of an array has the declared element type: an int[] holds only int values, a String[] only String references.

wrong rule: The number of brackets in an array type is the array's length. Right rule: Each bracket pair adds one dimension (int[] is 1-D, int[][] is 2-D); the length is not part of the type and is fixed only when the array is created.

Points to LT: declare, then create, then initialize, in that order. Inconsistent application: the trace treats a as already created on some lines (reading a[i] straight after 'int[] a;') while requiring new on others. (here mixing in: "int[] a; already makes an array that can be indexed")
wrong rule: X[i] names the whole array, not one element. Right rule: The name a (written a[] in the book) denotes the whole array; a[i] denotes the single element at index i.

Conservation: rewriting 'int[] a' as 'int a[]' keeps the meaning. Changing the element type changes which values may be stored and the default values. Deleting the creation step breaks the program at compile time.
wrong rule: A comment line is run like a statement. Right rule: The compiler ignores comments: everything from // to the end of the line and everything between /* and */.

Applies the skip rule unevenly: skips one comment while tracing but 'executes' another (e.g. a commented-out println), or forgets that // ends at the line break. (here mixing in: "A comment line is run like a statement")
Adding, removing or editing a comment keeps behaviour unchanged, as long as the delimiters stay intact; deleting a closing */ or turning a statement into a comment changes the program.
wrong rule: An out-of-bounds read returns null (or 0). Right rule: Reading or writing any index outside 0 to a.length - 1 throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException and returns no value.

Points to LT: the bounds check runs at every access, at run time. Inconsistent application: the trace accepts an index of a.length on the last pass (or -1 on the first) but rejects it elsewhere, or reads 'some value' there. (here mixing in: "an out-of-bounds read returns null (it throws)")

wrong rule: < vs <= and 0..n vs 0..n-1 are interchangeable. Right rule: for (i = 0; i < n; i++) runs n times with i going up to n - 1; with <= it runs n + 1 times and reaches i = n, which is out of bounds for an array of length n.

Conservation: a loop bounded by i < a.length stays within bounds when the array size changes. Changing < to <= adds one pass that throws, and starting at 1 or ending at a.length-1 silently skips an element.

wrong rule: The class name and the file name are independent, so public class HelloWorld can be saved as hello.java or Program.java. Right rule: A public class Name must be saved in a file called exactly Name.java (same spelling and case).

Applies the reading rule (LT for program_text: the compiler reads the file Name.java character by character from top to bottom, ignoring comments and whitespace between tokens) unevenly: e.g. reads the code but also the comments as if they ran, or treats the file name as irrelevant on one pass and as the program name on another. (here mixing in: "class name and filename are independent")

wrong rule: The computer fills in steps or values the programmer meant but did not write. Right rule: The program text is all the computer has: it executes only what the code states, so every step and value must be written.

Renaming the class without renaming the file (or vice versa) breaks compilation; changing whitespace between tokens or editing comments keeps the behaviour unchanged; changing any character inside quotes changes the output.

wrong rule: a large integer literal is automatically long. Right rule: A sequence of digits is an int literal only if its value falls within the int range; for larger values the book advises the long type.
wrong rule: Java has no float literals. Right rule: A decimal literal ending in f is a float; without the f it is a double.
wrong rule: Java has no long literals. Right rule: An integer literal ending in L is a long.
wrong rule: 207. and 2.3e4 are int values because they are whole numbers. Right rule: A decimal point or scientific notation makes the literal a double.

Points to LT (each literal denotes one fixed value whose type is read from how it is written). Applied unevenly, a student reads 2.0 as an int in one place, or '7' as the number 7 in one expression and as a character in the next. (here mixing in: "a large integer literal is automatically long")
Rewriting a literal in another form keeps the value but changes the type, and so the operation: 10 / 3 is 3 but 10.0 / 3 is 3.333..., and "5" + 1 is "51" but 5 + 1 is 6.
wrong rule: A variable declared inside a block can be used anywhere in the program, like a global. Right rule: A local variable's scope runs from its declaration to the end of the enclosing block.

Applies the block rule (LT: all statements of the block in order, the whole block as one unit) unevenly: includes the statement after the closing brace in the body on one pass but not another, or runs only part of the body. (here mixing in: "A variable declared inside a block can be used anywhere in the program, like a global")

wrong rule: A statement placed after the if statement belongs to its branch, so it runs only when the condition is true. Right rule: The branch ends at its closing brace (or after its single statement); the next statement runs whatever the condition was.

wrong rule: Some statements inside the loop braces are not repeated; they run once, before or after the loop. Right rule: Every statement inside the loop braces is part of the body and runs on every pass.

wrong rule: A statement written after the loop is repeated with the loop body. Right rule: The body ends at the closing brace (or after its single statement); code after it runs once, after the loop ends.

Adding braces around a single-statement body keeps behaviour; adding a second statement to a braceless body changes it (the new statement runs outside); moving a declaration into a block makes later uses outside the block fail to compile.
wrong rule: a reference variable holds the whole object, not a reference. Right rule: A reference variable holds only a reference to the object, which is stored separately.
wrong rule: A variable can contain more than one value. Right rule: A variable holds exactly one value at a time; assigning a new value replaces the old one.

wrong rule: The computer recognises that one variable plays two roles, e.g. input value and running total, and keeps the values apart; it knows which variable is the counter and which the sum. Right rule: A variable holds one value at a time; each role (input, counter, running total) needs its own variable and explicit update.
wrong rule: A variable keeps its first value after a new assignment (the static model). Right rule: Each assignment or read replaces the variable's current value.

Points to LT (a read gives the current value, and each assignment replaces it). Applied unevenly, a student updates the value after some assignments but keeps the first value after others, or switches between a memory model and an equation model across tasks (y = x - y read as x = 2y). (here mixing in: "a reference variable holds the whole object, not a reference")
wrong rule: A variable declared inside a block can be used anywhere in the program, like a global. Right rule: A local variable exists only from its declaration to the end of its block.

wrong rule: a variable declared in the loop body lives across all iterations. Right rule: A variable declared inside the body is created anew on every pass and does not keep the previous pass's value.

wrong rule: Naming a variable max (or average) makes it hold the largest value (or the average) without code that computes it. Right rule: A name only labels the variable for human readers; only the statements that assign to it decide its value.
wrong rule: = stores the expression itself, not its computed value. Right rule: y = x + k; stores the value that x + k has at that moment, so later changes to x do not change y.

wrong rule: A variable declared int can hold 2.5 or "hi"; the type is only a label. Right rule: A data type is a set of values and a set of operations defined on them, so an int variable holds only int values.
wrong rule: local variables get a default value on their own. Right rule: A local variable has no value until it is assigned, and using it before then does not compile.
wrong rule: keywords may be reused as identifiers. Right rule: Keywords are reserved by Java and cannot be used as variable names.

wrong rule: int x; without a value sets aside no memory; the variable only exists once something is assigned. Right rule: A declaration creates the variable (its storage) with its type; assignment later puts a value in it.
wrong rule: Reading a second input value into a variable that already holds one is an error, so the program cannot run. Right rule: A later read simply overwrites the variable's current value.

wrong rule: An array element a[i] is not a variable, so it cannot be read into directly or used inside another index, as in a[a[i]]. Right rule: Each element a[i] is a variable of the element type and can be used anywhere a variable of that type can, including as an index.

Renaming a variable consistently keeps behavior. Reordering statements that write and read it changes results (a = b; b = a; is not a swap). Moving its declaration into a loop body narrows its scope and resets it on every pass.
wrong rule: i and a[i] are the same thing, so the position is the stored value. Right rule: i is a position; a[i] is the value stored at that position.
wrong rule: The first element of a is a[1]. Right rule: Numbering begins with 0; the first element is a[0].
wrong rule: new int[n] has slots 0 to n, inclusive. Right rule: The slots are 0 to n - 1.
wrong rule: a(i) accesses element i of an array. Right rule: Array elements are selected with square brackets, a[i]; a(i) would be a call of a method named a.

wrong rule: An array element a[i] is not a variable, so it cannot be read into directly or used inside another index, as in a[a[i]]. Right rule: Each element a[i] is a variable of the element type and can be used anywhere a variable of that type can, including as an index.
wrong rule: X[i] names the whole array, not one element. Right rule: The array is a (a[] in the book); a[i] is the single element at index i.
wrong rule: After i changes, X[i] still refers to the element at the old value of i. Right rule: a[i] is evaluated with the current value of i each time it is executed.

Points to LT: in a[i], a is evaluated, then i with its current value, then the bounds check, then the element is read or written. Inconsistent application: i is updated on one line, but a later a[i] is traced with the old i. (here mixing in: "i and a[i] are the same thing, so the position is the stored value")
wrong rule: Using an array means every cell must be scanned. Right rule: Arrays allow random access: a[i] reaches one element directly, and a loop visits only the elements the task needs.

Conservation: changing the index expression (i to i+1 or i-1) shifts which element is touched and can leave the bounds at the ends. Writing a[a[i]] instead of a[i] uses an element value as the index, a different access entirely. Changing what is stored never changes the positions.
wrong rule: a string literal isn't a String object until the constructor is called. Right rule: A string literal is already a String object, so "text".length() works directly.
wrong rule: .equals() compares references, not contents. Right rule: s.equals(t) checks whether the two Strings contain the same characters.

wrong rule: "10" - 1 or "6" * "2" works because the strings look like numbers. Right rule: Arithmetic operators other than + are not defined for Strings; a String of digits must first be converted to a number, e.g. with Integer.parseInt.

Points to LT (String expressions produce references to String objects, and operations build new strings). Applied unevenly, a student compares with equals in one test and == in another, or treats "12" as a number in one + and as text in the next. (here mixing in: "a string literal isn't a String object until the constructor is called")
wrong rule: String is a primitive type like int. Right rule: String is not a primitive type; it is a class whose values are objects, although Java gives it some built-in support (literals, +).
wrong rule: == compares contents (the String == bug). Right rule: s == t is true only when s and t refer to the same object; s.equals(t) compares the text.
wrong rule: s < t compares two Strings alphabetically. Right rule: < and > are defined only for primitive types; comparing Strings with them does not compile.
Replacing equals with == may still pass for two identical literals but fails for computed or input strings. Changing "5" to 5 turns concatenation into addition.
wrong rule: Command-line arguments arrive already typed as numbers, so no parsing is needed. Right rule: args[0] is always a String, so Integer.parseInt(args[0]) is needed to get its number.

Applies the args rule unevenly: maps the first typed word to args[0] on one run but to args[1] on another, or treats a numeric argument as a String in one place and as an int in another. (here mixing in: "command-line args arrive already typed, no parsing needed")
Changing the typed arguments changes the output but not the program; typing fewer arguments than the program reads causes ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException; extra arguments are ignored unless read.

wrong rule: System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method. Right rule: Java is case-sensitive: names of variables, methods and classes that differ only in capitalization are different names.
wrong rule: keywords may be reused as identifiers. Right rule: Keywords are reserved by Java and cannot be used as variable names.

Points to LT (a name refers to the declaration with exactly that spelling in scope). Applied unevenly, a student treats Count and count as one variable in one statement but as two in another. (here mixing in: "System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method")

Renaming an identifier consistently at its declaration and every use leaves behavior unchanged. Renaming only some occurrences, or changing only the capitalization, breaks compilation with 'cannot find symbol'.
wrong rule: Code that compiles is code that works. Right rule: Code that compiles can still fail at run time (an exception) or give wrong output.
wrong rule: System.out.println(5 / 0); is rejected by the compiler. Right rule: It compiles; integer division by zero throws ArithmeticException when the statement runs.

Applies the exception rule (LT: execution stops at the faulty statement) unevenly: lets the program keep printing after the failing statement on one trace, or reports the error before any earlier output on another. (here mixing in: "Code that compiles is code that works")
wrong rule: Integer.parseInt works on any text, e.g. "five" or "12.2". Right rule: Integer.parseInt throws a NumberFormatException at run time when the string is not an integer written in digits.

The same compiled program may run fine on one input and throw on another (UseArgument with and without an argument); adding a guard such as checking args.length removes the trigger without changing correct runs.
wrong rule: Code that compiles is code that works. Right rule: Compiling only checks the language rules; code that compiles can still have run-time and logic errors.

wrong rule: The line number in a javac error is always the line that has the mistake. Right rule: The compiler reports where it noticed the problem, which can be after the real fault (omitting HelloWorld's second left brace gives errors on later lines).

Applies the 'javac checks before running' rule unevenly: predicts output for a program that would not compile, or expects a compile error from a fault (such as division by zero) that only shows at run time. (here mixing in: "Code that compiles is code that works")

wrong rule: Doing exactly what the compiler message suggests will fix the error. Right rule: An error message is evidence that something is wrong, but its suggested remedy may be wrong; find the actual cause.
Fixing the first error and recompiling can remove many messages at once; a single missing brace or semicolon can cause several messages.
wrong rule: + with a String turns the whole other side into a string first. Right rule: The expression (a + b) is evaluated first, and its value is then turned into text and joined to s.
wrong rule: 2 + 3 + "bc" and "bc" + 2 + 3 give the same text. Right rule: + is evaluated left to right: 2 + 3 + "bc" is "5bc" but "bc" + 2 + 3 is "bc23".

Points to LT (left to right, and each + adds or concatenates according to its operands at that moment). Applied unevenly, a student keeps adding numbers after a String has appeared, or concatenates before any String appears (1 + 2 + "x" as "12x"). (here mixing in: "+ with a String turns the whole other side into a string first")

wrong rule: arithmetic + binds tighter than string-concatenation +. Right rule: Both uses of + have the same precedence and are evaluated left to right, so "s" + a + b joins a and then b as text; only "s" + (a + b) adds them first.

Parenthesizing numeric parts changes the result ("sum " + (a + b) adds before joining). Moving numbers before or after the first String changes whether they are added. Concatenating into a printf format string removes the separate argument printf needs.
